name: Second Battle of El Alamein
info: Eighth Army under Lieutenant-General Bernard Montgomery broke the fortified Axis line at El Alamein in Egypt in a 13-day battle, defeating Rommel's Panzer Army Africa and forcing it to retreat from Egypt and Libya to the borders of Tunisia.

facts.date: 23 October – 4 November 1942 (a 13-day battle; the Axis retreat and the Allied pursuit continued to 11 November)
facts.place: Near the railway halt of El Alamein on the Mediterranean coast of Egypt, on a front between the sea and the Qattara Depression, about 50 miles (80 km) from Alexandria
facts.sides: The British Commonwealth Eighth Army under Lieutenant-General Bernard Montgomery, with 195,000 men and 1,029 tanks; the German-Italian Panzer Army (Panzerarmee Afrika) under Field Marshal Erwin Rommel, with 116,000 men and 547 tanks
facts.outcome: The Axis defences were broken and Panzerarmee Afrika was forced to retreat from Egypt and Libya; most of the Italian infantry, which lacked transport, was abandoned. The victory ended the Axis threat to the Middle East and Iran.

t: Montgomery planned a battle of attrition in which his superiority in men, tanks, guns and aircraft would 'crumble' the Axis defences; he expected it to last 12 days, and it lasted 13.

Axis fuel was short throughout: by 25 October Panzerarmee Afrika had three days' supply, only two days' of it east of Tobruk, and tankers carrying fuel were sunk at the end of October and in early November.

Casualty figures differ by source: Eighth Army lost 13,560 men, while Axis losses are put at 36,939 in one reckoning that Niall Barr calls very uncertain, and as much larger totals once the retreat is counted.
dyk: Before the attack Eighth Army hid its build-up in the north with dummy dumps under camouflage nets, dummy tanks and guns of calico and palm-frond hurdles in the south, real tanks disguised as trucks with plywood superstructures, and a dummy water pipeline built slowly enough to suggest it would not be finished until after the attack.
ev: Panzer Army Africa wins the Battle of Gazala and advances into Egypt
Axis attacks in the First Battle of El Alamein are defeated
Churchill and Brooke replace Auchinleck with Alexander, and Montgomery takes command of Eighth Army
Rommel's attack is repulsed at the Alam el Halfa ridge
Operation Lightfoot opens with a barrage of 1,000 guns
Operation Supercharge begins, and the 9th Armoured Brigade attacks the Axis gun line; on 4 November the Axis front is broken and Rommel orders a retreat
Eighth Army takes Tripoli as Rommel withdraws to the Mareth Line

sections.background:
After its success at Gazala, Panzer Army Africa, made up of German and Italian units under Erwin Rommel, advanced into Egypt and threatened British control of the Suez Canal, the Middle East and its oil resources. General Claude Auchinleck withdrew Eighth Army to within 50 miles (80 km) of Alexandria, to the El Alamein line, where the Qattara Depression, 40 miles (64 km) to the south, was impassable and any attack had to be frontal. Axis attacks in the First Battle of El Alamein (1–27 July) were defeated, and Eighth Army counter-attacks in July also failed.

In early August Winston Churchill and General Sir Alan Brooke visited Cairo and replaced Auchinleck as Commander-in-Chief Middle East Command with General Harold Alexander. Lieutenant-General William Gott, made commander of Eighth Army, was killed when his transport aircraft was shot down, and Lieutenant-General Bernard Montgomery was flown from Britain to replace him. Rommel, lacking reinforcements, dependent on small ports for supplies and aware of a huge Allied reinforcement, attacked first, but was repulsed at the Alam el Halfa ridge on 30 August 1942.

The short front and secure flanks favoured the defence, and Rommel used the time to sow minefields of about 500,000 mines, with miles of barbed wire. Alexander and Montgomery intended to build a superiority of force sufficient for a breakthrough that could be exploited to destroy Panzerarmee Afrika. Earlier in the campaign neither side had been able to exploit a local victory enough to defeat its opponent before it withdrew.
sections.forces:
After six more weeks of preparation Eighth Army was ready, with 195,000 men and 1,029 tanks against the 116,000 men and 547 tanks of the Panzerarmee. It drew men and materials from the United Kingdom, India, Australia and New Zealand, and Sherman tanks from the United States. Montgomery's plan, Operation Lightfoot, was a main attack in the north by XXX Corps (Lieutenant-General Oliver Leese) and a secondary attack in the south by XIII Corps (Lieutenant-General Brian Horrocks), while X Corps (Lieutenant-General Herbert Lumsden) was to exploit the success. He expected a 12-day battle in three stages: the break-in, the dogfight and the final breaking of the enemy.

Under Operation Bertram the British deceived the Axis about where and when the attack would fall. Rommel was ill and left for Germany on 23 September, and General der Panzertruppe Georg Stumme took his place. The defences were laid out in at least two belts of mines about 3.1 miles (5 km) apart, linked into boxes known as Devil's gardens, and the forward lines alternated German and Italian infantry formations.

Rommel did not want the British armour to reach open ground, since he had neither the numbers nor the fuel for a battle of manoeuvre. Because the deception left him unsure where the blow would come, he split his armour into a northern group (15th Panzer Division and the Littorio Division) and a southern group (21st Panzer Division and the Ariete Division). The 15th Panzer Division had 125 operational tanks and the 21st Panzer Division 121.
sections.course:
At 21:40 on 23 October, Operation Lightfoot began with a 1,000-gun barrage, which went on for five and a half hours and used about 529,000 shells. The four infantry divisions of XXX Corps advanced from 22:00, but the minefields were deeper than expected, clearing them was slow, and the tanks raised so much dust and jammed so badly that none broke through. Only about half of the infantry reached their objectives. On 24 October Stumme suffered a heart attack and died, and Major-General Wilhelm Ritter von Thoma took temporary command. At dusk on the 24th the first big tank engagement began at the Kidney feature, with over 100 tanks involved; half were destroyed by dark.

Montgomery shifted his main effort north with the 9th Australian Division, while Rommel ordered the 90th Light Division and the 21st Panzer Division north, a move that fuel shortage made impossible to reverse. On 27 October at Snipe the Rifle Brigade, with thirteen 6-pounder anti-tank guns and six more, held off tank attacks and destroyed 22 German and 10 Italian tanks. On 28 October the 15th and 21st Panzer Divisions attacked again but were halted, Rommel's last attempt to take the initiative.

Operation Supercharge began at 01:00 on 2 November with a barrage of 360 guns firing 15,000 shells. The 9th Armoured Brigade attacked at 06:15 with 94 runners and was reduced to 24, and 230 of the 400 men involved were killed, wounded or captured; it did not open the gap, but the Axis counter-attack at 11:00 failed at a cost of about 100 tanks. On 3 November Hitler ordered Rommel to stand fast. On 4 November the Axis front was broken and at 17:30 Rommel ordered a retreat.
sections.aftermath:
Because of lack of transport most of the Italian infantry formations were abandoned, since Hitler's insistence that Rommel hold his ground had obliged him to keep the non-motorised Italian units forward until it was too late. The Ariete Armoured Division was destroyed in a determined resistance on 4 November, and the Littorio and Trieste Divisions were also destroyed. The Bologna Division and the remnants of the Trento Division marched into the desert without water, food or transport before surrendering, exhausted and dying from dehydration. By 11 November Axis prisoners numbered 30,000.

Eighth Army was surprised by the withdrawal and was slow in pursuit, failing to cut off Rommel at Fuka and Mersa Matruh. The 1st Armoured Division ran out of fuel, rain on 6 November bogged down a fuel convoy, and waterlogged ground and lack of fuel stranded two armoured divisions on 7 November. On 11 November the 5th New Zealand Infantry Brigade captured the Halfaya Pass, taking 600 Italian prisoners, and the Egyptian frontier was clear.

Eighth Army had 13,560 casualties: 2,350 killed, 8,950 wounded and 2,260 missing. It lost from 332 to 500 tanks, 300 of which had been repaired by the end of the battle. British figures based on Ultra give German casualties as 1,149 killed, 3,886 wounded and 8,050 captured, and Italian losses as 971 dead, 933 wounded and 15,552 captured. About 500 Axis tanks were lost. The Axis then withdrew by stages through El Agheila to Tripoli, which fell on 23 January 1943, and on to the Mareth Line in Tunisia.
sections.sources:
Much of what is known of the Axis side comes from Rommel's own signals and diary, quoted in the histories, and from Fritz Bayerlein's notes to The Rommel Papers. For the British, Ultra decrypts and local sources exposed the Axis order of battle, supply position and intentions, so that supply ships could be found and attacked. Until the end of June 1942 Rommel had in turn read detailed reports on British forces sent to Washington by the United States military attaché in Cairo, Colonel Bonner Fellers, because the American code had been stolen. Lucas-Phillips's Alamein and the regimental histories give the view from the units that fought.

The casualty figures vary between sources. Niall Barr wrote in 2005 that the figure of 36,939 for Panzerarmee casualties was very uncertain because of the chaos of the Axis retreat. Bayerlein estimated German losses at 1,100 killed, 3,900 wounded and 7,900 prisoners and Italian losses at 1,200 killed, 1,600 wounded and 20,000 prisoners. The Italian official history gives Axis losses in the battle as 4,000 to 5,000 killed or missing, 7,000 to 8,000 wounded and 17,000 prisoners, rising during the retreat to 9,000 killed or missing, 15,000 wounded and 35,000 prisoners.

Historians debate why Rommel advanced into Egypt. In 1997 Martin van Creveld wrote that German and Italian staffs had advised that his army could not be supplied so far from Tripoli and Benghazi. According to Maurice Remy (2002), Hitler and Mussolini pressed him to advance in order to take the Suez Canal and the Middle Eastern oil fields.
sections.legacy:
The Allied victory at El Alamein was the beginning of the end of the Western Desert Campaign. It ended the Axis threat to the Middle East and Iran, and revived the morale of the western Allies as their first large success against the Axis since Operation Crusader in late 1941. Its end coincided with the Allied landing in French North Africa in Operation Torch on 8 November. Italian and German forces in North Africa capitulated in May 1943.

Alexander suggested to Churchill that he ring out the bells. Speaking at the Lord Mayor's Banquet on 10 November 1942, Churchill emphasised the victory's importance but warned against premature celebration: 'This is not the end. It is not even the beginning of the end. But it is perhaps the end of the beginning.' In his memoirs in 1950 he wrote that 'Before Alamein we never had a victory. After Alamein we never had a defeat'.

The battle is remembered for episodes within it. The regimental historian of the Rifle Brigade called the action at Snipe the most famous day of the regiment's war, and its commanding officer, Lieutenant-Colonel Victor Buller Turner, was awarded the Victoria Cross. Rommel wrote that the Italians of the Ariete fought with exemplary courage. Montgomery had foreseen an attrition battle and accurately predicted its length and the number of British and Commonwealth casualties.

summary: At El Alamein in October and November 1942 Montgomery's Eighth Army, with 195,000 men and 1,029 tanks, broke the fortified line held by Rommel's 116,000 men and 547 tanks after 13 days of attrition. The Axis army retreated from Egypt and Libya to the borders of Tunisia.
references: Field Marshal Lord Carver, El Alamein (Wordsworth Editions, 2000)
notes: The article's 'Prelude' says 'Rommel decided to advance into Egypt' after Alam el Halfa, which contradicts its own account of the Axis going onto the defensive; I left it out.

'Lumsden wanted to call off the attack planned for the night of 24/25 September' is plainly October; I did not use it. The article gives the Australian casualties of the 28/29 October attack twice and inconsistently ('200 casualties' and '27 killed and 290 wounded'); left out.
The 'drunken negroes with tanks' remark is quoted in the article of an Italian unit's message; left out as slur and not needed.

The article has no legacy or sources section; the legacy and sources sections are built from the Analysis, Casualties, Background and quotation material, and the Ultra/Fellers intelligence passage. The sources section is therefore about how the figures and intelligence reached us rather than a survey of historiography.
Axis tank figures: 'about 500' Axis tanks lost appears in the article beside Rizzo's 510; I give 'about 500' only. The Eighth Army tank loss is given as a range, 332 to 500.
Montgomery's expected length was 12 days; the article calls the battle 13 days. Stated both.
Axis casualty total in the first takeaway: 36,939 is the figure Barr calls uncertain; the article does not say whose count it is.
Phase wording 'Rommel held for a day' summarises the 3 November order and the Afrika Korps withdrawal of about 6 miles that night; it is a summary, not a quotation.
The Italian XX Corps, the Folgore stand at Deir el Munassib (Operation Braganza) and Thoma's capture were left out for length.
